At the same temperature, for the same physical property and under the same measurement conditions, an object's property changes with the direction of measurement. Is this anisotropy alone enough to conclude that the object must be crystalline?
In your discussion, distinguish single crystals, polycrystalline materials with randomly oriented grains or a preferred grain orientation, and amorphous materials with directional internal structure or applied stress. Do not use differences in an object's external shape as evidence of an internal crystal structure.

Suppose glass were replaced by a crystalline material with a definite melting point and no continuous softening range below that point, unlike ordinary glass. Would this necessarily mean that glassblowing could no longer exist as an occupation?
Distinguish working a material in a softened state from working it as a liquid after melting. Classifying a material as "crystalline" does not specify its melt viscosity, crystallization rate, or the conditions needed to retain its shape after blowing. This is only a hypothetical discussion of materials processing; do not carry out high-temperature glassblowing.

At ordinary room temperature, are solid table sugar, amber, and aluminum crystalline or amorphous?
Discuss common samples. Here, table sugar means ordinary granulated sugar, not specially prepared glassy sugar. The crystalline category includes both single crystals and polycrystalline materials; the presence or absence of complete external crystal faces is not the sole criterion.

Table-salt crystals consist of alternating sodium and chloride ions and often have a cubic external shape; see Figure 77. The figure illustrates only the crystal's external appearance and provides neither ion positions nor a distance scale.
Use an ideal rock-salt structure model: treat the centers of all ions of both types as equally spaced sites on a three-dimensional simple-cubic lattice, with sodium and chloride ions alternating along each cubic axis. The sites of each type form two interpenetrating face-centered cubic sublattices. Find the average center-to-center distance between nearest neighboring ions of different types, not the average distance between arbitrary pairs of ions.
The molar mass of table salt is 0.058 kilograms/mole, and its density is 2200 kilograms/meter$^3$. The molar mass refers to formula units, each containing one sodium ion and one chloride ion. The total number of ions per unit volume is therefore twice the density multiplied by the Avogadro constant and divided by the molar mass. These structural and counting assumptions are part of the stipulated model, not measurements read from the image of the crystal's exterior.

Use a model with uniform axial stress across a circular cross section, neglecting the rod's own weight. What static force must be applied along the axis to produce a stress of $15\times10^7$ newtons/meter$^2$ in the rod?
The load passes through the center of the cross section, and bending is neglected. The rod's diameter is 0.4 centimeters.

6. A vertical brick wall is 20 meters high. In a model with uniform wall density and a cross-sectional area that does not vary with height, and with only the wall's own weight acting, what average compressive stress does the base of the wall exert on the foundation?
The density of the brick is 1800 kilograms/meter$^3$. Neglect mortar, external loads, foundation settlement, and similar effects. If bricks are selected to support the weight of the wall above each location, must the required compressive strength be the same at the base and in the upper part of the wall? This question only compares loading requirements; it is not a basis for building design.

7. A uniform steel wire is fixed at its upper end and hangs vertically with its lower end free and no additional weight attached. In an ideal model with constant cross-sectional area, only the wire's own weight acting, and defects and vibrations neglected, what is the minimum wire length at which the breaking condition is reached?
The ultimate tensile strength of the steel is $3.2\times10^8$ newtons/meter$^2$, and its density is 7800 kilograms/meter$^3$. This is a theoretical estimate; do not carry out an experiment involving a long suspended wire or breaking a wire.

8. A uniform wire is 5 meters long and has a cross-sectional area of 2.5 millimeters$^2$. A static tensile force of 100 newtons applied along its axis produces an extension of 1 millimeter.
Assume the deformation is within the linear elastic range, the load passes through the center of the cross section, and the wire's own weight and temperature changes are negligible. Find the stress and Young's modulus of the wire.

9. In an ideal energy-conversion model, a bullet stops after striking a wall, and all its initial kinetic energy goes only into heating and melting the bullet itself. No heat is transferred to the wall or surroundings, and no other energy pathways are included. What speed immediately before impact would make the bullet just melt completely?
The bullet material has a melting point of $600\text{K}$, a specific heat capacity of 125 joules/(kilogram·degree), and a latent heat of fusion per unit mass of $2.5\times10^4$ joules/kilogram. The bullet's temperature before impact is $50^\circ\text{C}$.
Assume the specific heat capacity is independent of temperature. The "degree" in its unit denotes a Celsius temperature difference, numerically equal to the corresponding kelvin temperature difference; convert to a common temperature scale before calculating the temperature rise. This is only a theoretical calculation; do not carry out shooting or impact experiments.

10. To cool 0.2 kilograms of water initially at $23^\circ\text{C}$ to $8^\circ\text{C}$, add small pieces of ice initially at $-3^\circ\text{C}$. What mass of ice must be added?
Assume ordinary atmospheric pressure, a container thermally insulated from its surroundings, negligible heat absorbed or released by the container itself, no evaporation or splashing, and a final state of thermal equilibrium. Include the warming of the ice, its melting, and the warming of the resulting water, using the specific heat capacities and latent heat of fusion given in this chapter.

11. A thermally insulated container holds water at $0^\circ\text{C}$ with a mass of 0.5 kilograms and ice at $0^\circ\text{C}$ with a mass of 54.4 grams. Steam with a mass of 6.6 grams and a temperature of $100^\circ\text{C}$ is introduced. What is the temperature in the container after thermal equilibrium is reached?
Use a heat-balance model at ordinary atmospheric pressure. Assume all the introduced steam condenses and remains in the container, and neglect heat absorbed or released by the container, heat exchange with the surroundings, and changes in macroscopic mechanical energy. Use the specific heat capacities of water and ice and the latent heats of fusion and vaporization given in this chapter. Determine from the energy balance whether any ice remains; do not assume that all the ice has melted.
